organic:oc-1iyt40m.w: The ketone comes back racemic. The stereocenter is an alpha carbon with a hydrogen, so hydroxide removes that hydrogen to make a flat enolate, and the proton returns to either face equally.
s: The stereocenter is **alpha** to the C=O and holds an H.
Hydroxide removes it: a flat, **sp2 enolate**.
The stereocenter's handedness is gone.
Water puts the H back on **either face**: 50:50 R and S.
t: Haloform cleavage needs a halogen (I2, Br2 or Cl2) with the base. None is present.
The carbonyl carbon stays a C=O. No new stereocenter is made there.
Enolization does happen toward the methyl, but it also happens at the stereocenter, whose hydrogen is even more acidic because of the phenyl.
Hydroxide removes a proton here; it does not displace anything. Backside inversion is an SN2 idea and needs a leaving group.
c: Would (R)-3-methyl-3-phenylpentan-2-one racemize in base?
No. Its alpha stereocenter has no hydrogen, so it cannot form that enolate.

organic:oc-o828tv.w: The product is cyclohexylacetaldehyde. Hydroboration puts the oxygen on the end carbon of the alkyne, the enol that forms tautomerizes, and an OH on a terminal carbon gives an aldehyde.
s: Boron adds to the **end carbon** of the alkyne.
Peroxide swaps boron for OH: an **enol**.
The enol **tautomerizes** to a carbonyl.
Carbonyl on the end carbon: an **aldehyde**, ring-CH2-CHO.
t: This aldehyde has the CHO directly on the ring. That loses a carbon; the alkyne's two carbons both stay.
The methyl ketone is the Markovnikov product, made with Hg(II) and aqueous acid.
The alcohol would need a further reduction. Hydroboration-oxidation of an alkyne stops at the carbonyl.
The enol is the intermediate. It does not survive; it tautomerizes to the aldehyde.
c: Which reagents give the methyl ketone from this alkyne?
H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4.

organic:oc-1usu1iz.w: NaBH4 in methanol, then acid workup. Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon and gives the primary alcohol without adding any carbon.
s: Aldehyde to primary alcohol is a **reduction**.
No new carbon: the nucleophile must be **hydride**.
NaBH4 delivers H- to the carbonyl carbon.
Protonation gives **PhCH2OH**.
t: Hot KMnO4 oxidizes the aldehyde to benzoic acid, the opposite direction.
A methyl Grignard adds a carbon and gives 1-phenylethanol, a secondary alcohol.
Methyllithium also adds a methyl group: a new C-C bond and a secondary alcohol.
A phenyl Grignard adds a second ring and gives diphenylmethanol.
c: What does NaBH4 do to an ester under these conditions?
Essentially nothing. Esters need LiAlH4.

organic:oc-ym5nrn.w: 1-Bromopropane. With peroxides HBr adds by a radical chain: the bromine atom adds to the end carbon to leave the more stable secondary radical, so Br ends up on the terminal carbon.
s: Peroxides start a **radical chain**.
A Br atom adds to the **CH2 end**: a secondary radical.
The radical takes H from HBr.
Br on C1: **anti-Markovnikov**.
t: Two bromines come from Br2. HBr adds one hydrogen and one bromine.
Allyl bromide keeps the double bond. That is allylic substitution, done with NBS.
2-Bromopropane is the Markovnikov product, formed when no peroxide is present.
An alcohol needs water or hydroxide. Neither is present.
c: What is the product without the peroxide?
2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov).

organic:oc-1g5ezpj.w: I, then II, then III. The alkene has to lie flat on the metal surface, and each extra substituent gets in the way, so the least substituted alkene is hydrogenated fastest.
s: Hydrogenation happens on the **metal surface**.
The C=C must lie **flat** against it.
More substituents: more **crowding**, slower uptake.
Mono (I) is fastest, tetra (III) slowest.
t: This is the stability order. The most substituted alkene is the most stable and the slowest to react.
The tetrasubstituted alkene is the most crowded, so it cannot beat the disubstituted one.
Cyclohexene is disubstituted, so it is slower than the monosubstituted 1-hexene.
The tetrasubstituted alkene is the slowest, not the fastest.
c: Which of the three alkenes releases the least heat on hydrogenation?
III, the tetrasubstituted alkene. It is the most stable.

organic:oc-yuv7z3.w: Five. Degrees of unsaturation = (2C + 2 - H) / 2 = (16 + 2 - 8) / 2 = 5: four for the benzene ring (three pi bonds and one ring) and one for the vinyl C=C.
s: Formula: (2C + 2 - H) / 2.
Check on the structure: benzene ring = **4**.
Vinyl C=C = **1**. Total 5.
t: Three counts only the pi bonds of the ring. The ring itself is one more, and the vinyl group another.
Four is the benzene ring alone. The vinyl C=C adds one.
Six is one too many. Four for the ring plus one for the vinyl group is five.
Eight is the number of hydrogens, not the degrees of unsaturation.
c: How many degrees of unsaturation does C6H12 have?
One: a ring or a double bond.

own-organic:ace-0010.w: On opposite faces of the ring. The first bromine forms a three-membered bridge across one face, so bromide can only come in from the other face.
s: The alkene attacks Br2: a bridged **bromonium** ion.
The bridge covers **one face** of the ring.
Bromide attacks from the **other face**.
Result: trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane.
t: Each alkene carbon gets one bromine. Two on the same carbon would need a different mechanism.
Anti addition happens at room temperature. Heat is not needed.
Both bromines add. The bromide left over from the first step opens the bridge.
Same-face addition is blocked by the bridging bromine.
c: What forms if the solvent is water instead of dichloromethane?
The trans bromohydrin: water opens the bromonium ion.

organic:oc-wj81go.w: Acetyl chloride with AlCl3. The Lewis acid removes chloride to give the acylium ion, CH3CO+, which the ring attacks.
s: An **acetyl** group is CH3C=O.
Its source: **acetyl chloride**, CH3COCl.
AlCl3 pulls off chloride: the **acylium ion**.
Benzene attacks it; loss of H+ gives acetophenone.
t: Chloroethane with AlCl3 is an alkylation. It gives ethylbenzene, with no C=O.
Methanol and sulfuric acid do not make a carbon electrophile that benzene will attack.
Acetic acid with NaOH just gives sodium acetate. There is no electrophile.
PCC oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde. Nothing here attaches a carbon to the ring.
c: Why does acylation stop after one acyl group?
The C=O deactivates the ring, so the product is less reactive than benzene.

organic:oc-1khayk8.w: The product is the methyl ester with the stereocenter unchanged. Fischer esterification happens at the carbonyl carbon: methanol adds there and water leaves, and no bond to the alpha carbon is broken.
s: Acid protonates the **C=O**.
Methanol attacks the **carbonyl carbon**.
Water leaves: the **methyl ester**.
The alpha carbon's four bonds are untouched: **retention**.
t: This is the inverted configuration. Inversion would need a bond to the stereocenter to break, and none does.
This shows no stereochemistry, as if the center were scrambled. It keeps its configuration.
This is a straight chain with the phenyl on the end carbon. The carbon skeleton does not change in an esterification.
This is the ethyl ester. The alcohol used is methanol.
c: How do you push a Fischer esterification toward the ester?
Use excess alcohol or remove the water as it forms.

organic:oc-h6tsou.w: It is an ester: a strong C=O band near 1740 cm-1 and nothing from O-H or N-H. An ester carbonyl absorbs a little higher than a ketone's (about 1715), and an ester has no O-H or N-H bond.
s: Strong band near 1740: a **C=O**.
No band from 2500 to 3500: **no O-H, no N-H**.
That rules out acids, alcohols and amides with N-H.
1740 is high for a ketone and right for an **ester**.
t: N-H bands appear near 3300 cm-1, far from the C=O region, so they cannot hide under it. Amide C=O is also lower, near 1650 to 1690.
The drawn molecule has two oxygens and is an ester. A ketone C=O would sit lower, near 1715.
A carboxylic acid O-H is one of the strongest, broadest bands in IR. It cannot be missed.
A C-O single bond stretches near 1000 to 1300 cm-1. 1740 is a C=O.
c: Where does a carboxylic acid O-H appear?
As a very broad band from about 2500 to 3300 cm-1.

organic:oc-1gh36h6.w: It loses CO2 and gives acetone. In a beta-keto acid the ketone oxygen takes the acid hydrogen through a six-membered ring arrangement as CO2 leaves, and the enol formed becomes the ketone.
s: The C=O is **beta** to the COOH.
The ketone O takes the acid H through a **six-membered** ring.
**CO2** leaves; an enol forms.
The enol tautomerizes: **acetone**.
t: Beta-keto acids are among the least stable acids to heat. They lose CO2 on gentle warming.
Reduction needs a hydride source. Heat alone does not reduce anything.
Acetic acid has two carbons. Losing CO2 from a four-carbon acid leaves three: acetone.
An aldol needs base and gives a larger molecule. Heat here simply removes CO2.
c: Does butanoic acid lose CO2 on gentle heating?
No. It has no beta carbonyl to accept the proton.

organic:oc-105eytk.w: Cl2 in water. Chlorine forms a bridged chloronium ion, and water, the solvent, opens it from the back to give the trans chlorohydrin.
s: The alkene attacks Cl2: a bridged **chloronium** ion.
**Water** is the solvent, so it outnumbers chloride.
Water opens the bridge from the back.
Loss of H+: OH and Cl on **neighboring** carbons, trans.
t: Chloride ion is a nucleophile, and an alkene is one too. Salt water does not react with an alkene.
HCl adds H and Cl. It gives chlorocyclohexane, with no OH.
In concentrated NaOH, Cl2 is consumed by the base, and any chlorohydrin formed would close to the epoxide.
Without water, chloride opens the bridge and the product is the dichloride.
c: What does base do to a trans chlorohydrin?
It removes the OH proton and the alkoxide displaces chloride to give an epoxide.

organic:oc-12rz7w0.w: A primary alcohol, 1-hexanol. LiAlH4 reduces a carboxylic acid all the way; the aldehyde stage is more reactive than the acid and never survives.
s: LiAlH4 is a strong **hydride** donor.
It reduces the acid's carbonyl carbon.
The aldehyde formed on the way reacts **faster** than the acid.
Final product: RCH2OH, a **primary** alcohol.
t: LiAlH4 does reduce carboxylic acids. It is NaBH4 that leaves them alone.
A methyl ketone would need a new carbon. Hydride adds only hydrogen.
The aldehyde cannot be isolated with LiAlH4. It is reduced further at once.
A secondary alcohol would need a carbon nucleophile to add. The carbonyl carbon here ends up with two hydrogens.
c: Which hydride reagent leaves a carboxylic acid untouched?
NaBH4.

organic:oc-8s0vx8.w: 4-Nitrobenzoic acid. Hot permanganate oxidizes a methyl group on a benzene ring all the way to COOH and leaves the ring and the nitro group alone.
s: The methyl has **benzylic hydrogens**.
Hot KMnO4 oxidizes it fully: **COOH**.
The ring and the nitro group are untouched.
Acid workup gives 4-nitrobenzoic acid.
t: The aldehyde is easier to oxidize than the methyl group, so the reaction does not stop there.
The ring itself resists permanganate, but the benzylic methyl does not.
An amino group would need the nitro group reduced. Permanganate is an oxidant.
The alcohol is an early stage. Hot permanganate takes it on to the acid.
c: Which reagents would reduce the nitro group to NH2?
Sn or Fe with HCl, or H2 with Pd.

organic:oc-1gf08ol.w: E. On one alkene carbon Cl outranks the ethyl group, on the other Br outranks methyl, and Cl and Br are on opposite sides.
s: Rank by **atomic number** on each alkene carbon.
Left carbon: **Cl** over the ethyl carbon.
Right carbon: **Br** over the methyl carbon.
Cl and Br are on **opposite sides**: E.
t: The drawing fixes which side each group is on, so the geometry is defined.
A double bond is E or Z, never both.
Z would need Cl and Br on the same side. Rank by atomic number, not by size of the group.
Each alkene carbon holds two different groups, so E/Z isomers exist.
c: When are cis/trans labels not enough, so that E/Z is needed?
When the alkene carbons carry three or four different groups.
